analysis.one_liner: Imposes stiffer penalties on Medicare plans for abusive marketing and tells seniors which plans are repeat violators.
analysis.headline: The bill, aimed at protecting seniors from misleading Medicare plan marketing, sat in two House committees and died when the Congress ended without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Just as the new Medicare prescription drug benefit launched, this bill targeted private Medicare Advantage and drug plans that use misleading marketing to sign up seniors. It would count each piece of misleading mail, call, or email as a separate violation so fines add up, require the government to publicly name plans that keep getting sanctioned, let seniors trapped in a sanctioned plan switch to another one immediately, and order a government study of whether anti-fraud rules for these plans actually work.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors enrolled in or shopping for Medicare Advantage and Medicare prescription drug plans. The new Part D benefit had just launched and seniors were being bombarded with plan marketing; the bill would make repeat-offender plans easier to identify and easier to leave, and make deceptive pitches costlier for the plans that send them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors in Medicare Advantage and drug plans

how_it_helps.text: Each misleading piece of mail, phone call, email, or other marketing material would count as a separate violation, so penalties would scale with the size of a marketing campaign instead of being a one-time slap on the wrist [S2] [S3].

Each year starting in 2008, the government would have to mail every Medicare beneficiary a list of plans that received at least three sanctions in the prior two years, with the dates and types of each violation, and post that list online [S2] [S3].

Seniors enrolled in a plan whose enrollment is suspended for marketing or service failures would get a special window to switch to a different plan for the whole suspension period, instead of being locked in [S2] [S3].
The Comptroller General would study every anti-fraud and abuse rule applying to these plans, assess whether the rules and sanctions work, and report to Congress by May 2008 [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private insurers that offer Medicare Advantage and Medicare prescription drug plans, which would face much larger fines for marketing violations, public disclosure of repeat sanctions, and the compliance cost of cleaning up their marketing practices. To the extent fines and compliance costs bite, some of that could show up in plan premiums or plans exiting markets.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicare Advantage and drug plan insurers

drawbacks.text: Counting every mailer, call, or email as a separate violation is intentionally severe; a plan could rack up crippling penalties over technical errors in a large campaign, and critics of strict marketing enforcement argue that kind of penalty structure punishes paperwork mistakes the same as real deception [S3].
Publicly listing sanctioned plans could push some plans out of the market or raise premiums, reducing choices for seniors, particularly in areas with few plan options.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit for seniors — knowing which plans repeatedly broke marketing rules and being able to escape a bad plan — is direct and concrete. The main cost falls on insurers, which is the point of the bill, though the per-communication penalty design is blunt enough that a plan committing honest mistakes could face disproportionate fines. On balance the protections outweigh the enforcement costs, but the penalty mechanism is not finely tuned.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to a subcommittee, and neither committee ever acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Allyson Schwartz introduced the bill on December 18, 2005, with Rep. Nita Lowey as its one cosponsor [S1] [S3] [S4].
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction [S1] [S5].
On January 3, 2006 it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, and no further action was ever taken [S5].
The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and expired when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare Advantage and prescription drug plan insurers came out ahead: they faced no new penalties for abusive marketing, no public listing of repeat violators, and no requirement to release seniors trapped in sanctioned plans. The Medicare Part D marketing abuses the bill targeted continued to be addressed only by the existing, weaker enforcement rules.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan split was never tested; the bill's two sponsors were both Democrats, and the Republican-led committees to which it was referred took no action.

industries.note: The bill would have multiplied fines for misleading marketing and publicly named plans that repeatedly got sanctioned. Insurers used aggressive marketing to enroll seniors in plans that pay them per member, so disclosure and per-violation fines cut directly against that business practice.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D prescription drug plan sponsors
industries.note: The same penalty and disclosure rules would apply to prescription drug plans, and seniors in a suspended plan could leave immediately, taking premiums with them. The bill was written because seniors were being confused by the flood of plan marketing in the new Part D program's first year.
